card.field: paintless dent repair (PDR) for automotive bodies
card.role: PDR specialist / master technician who also instructs PDR training courses

sections.text:
A. Memberships
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2( o) (3 )(iii)(B)(2) requires "[d ]ocumentation ofthe alien's membership
in associations in the field for which classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of
their members, as judged by recognized national or international experts in their disciplines or fields."
USCIS determines ifthe association for which the person claims present or past membership requires that
members have outstanding achievements in the field as judged by recognized experts in the field. 3
At the outset, counsel's cover letters repeatedly claimed at initial filing and in the request for evidence
(RFE) response the Beneficiary's membership with "Automotive Repair Certification Association
(ARC)." However, the Petitioner did not present evidence reflecting the Beneficiary's membership with
"Automotive Repair Certification Association (ARC)." Instead, the Petitioner provided evidence of the
Beneficiary's status in PDR repair as a master technician with "ARC Certified."4 On appeal, counsel's
briefreferences the Beneficiary's membership with "ARC" without any mention of"Automotive Repair
Certification Association (ARC)." The record does not reflect the Beneficiary's membership with
"Automotive Repair Certification Association (ARC)," nor does the record show that such an association
even exists. Regardless, we will evaluate the Beneficiary's eligibility based on the evidence contained in
the record rather than unsupported assertions of counsel. See, e.g., Matter ofS-M-, 22 I&N Dec. 49, 51
users
1 See also generally 2 Policy Manual, M.4(C)(2), https://www.uscis.gov/policymanual.
2 Any ground of ineligibility that is not raised on appeal is waived. See Matter ofO-R-E-, 28 T&N Dec. 330. 336 n.5 (BIA
2021) (citing Matter ofR-A-M-, 25 T&N Dec. 657,658 n.2 (BIA 2012)).
3 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
4 ARC Certified, LLC is a registered business entity in Tennessee, see tncab.tnsos.gov.
2
(BIA 1998) ("statements in a brief, motion, or Notice of Appeal are not evidence and thus are not
entitled to any evidentiary weight").
Again, the Petitioner submitted evidence showing that the Beneficiary is an ARC Certified PDR repair
master technician. In addition, the Petitioner offered screenshots from ARC Certified reflecting:
• ARC is a not for profit organization based in the U.S. (Tennessee) and is open to all
qualifying U.S. PDR technicians irrespective of affiliation or brand.
• Multiple repairs, verified by multiple expert peers and ARC panel members, is the key
component to the ARC Verification.
• 3-5 referrals from Expert Hail response technicians. Candidates enlist these referrals
from expert technicians with whom they have worked multiple transactions using an
assigned URL code.
• 3-5 Complex (non-hail) work examples. Confirmation from our expert panel
members involves scoring: difficulty, results, presentation, angles and lighting used
in each example: At least 3 examples must score an Ml rating from our panel
members.
• Panel experts are chosen from highly skilled and proven PDR professionals across the
United States.
• The Verification Process, home or office plaque, and placement into the ARC registry
has a one-time fee.
Further, the Petitioner submitted a letter from J-D-, an owner and operator of a PDR business in Texas,
who stated:
I am personally familiar with this process because I am also a certified member of ARC.
The evaluation is based on actual repair work, not written tests or resumes. Applicants
must submit multiple examples of completed repairs on complex, non-routine damage.
These are typically dents involving body lines, edges, reinforced areas, or aluminum
panels; repairs where mistakes cannot be hidden.
Each repair is documented under controlled lighting and from multiple angles to expose
any distortion, tool marks, or imperfections in the metal. Reviewers look closely at how
the metal was moved, whether the original shape was fully restored, and whether the repair
remains invisible under harsh inspection lighting. Consistency across all submitted
repairs is critical; a single weak repair can result in rejection.
The evaluation is performed by experienced PDR technicians who work at a high level
themselves and understand how difficult these repairs are. In my experience, the process
is intentionally strict. It is designed to confirm that the technician can repeat elite-level
results, not just succeed once.
Although ARC Certified offers two certificates (hail repair and master technician), the Petitioner did not
demonstrate that ARC Certified requires outstanding achievements as a condition for certification.
Rather, a candidate must conduct verified "multiple repairs," possess "3-5 referrals," and provide work
examples, in which at least 3 must score an Ml rating. While ARC Certified may indicate a level of
3
competency to perform PDR, the Petitioner did not establish that such qualification represents
"outstanding achievements" consistent with this regulatory criterion. Cf, Kumar v. Dir. of US.
Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., No. CV RDB-23-2251, 2024 WL 1374794, at *5 (D. Md. Apr. 1, 2024)
(upholding plaintiff's documentation did not reflect that membership requires outstanding
achievements).
Furthermore, the Petitioner did not show that recognized national or international experts judge
membership. The screenshots reference "expert panel," "highly skilled," and "PDR professionals," and
J-D- indicates "experienced PDR technicians." However, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the panel is
comprised ofrecognized national or international experts. Without further information on the individuals
serving on the panel, including their identification, background, and national or international recognition,
the Petitioner did not establish the panel consists of national or international experts in their disciplines
or fields. Cf, Kim v. Mullin, No. 9:24-CV-80834-BER, 2026 WL 1512990, at *5 (S.D. Fla. Apr. 7,
2026) (upholding documents did not show that recognized national or international experts judged the
plaintiff as having outstanding achievements in the field); Kumar, 2024 WL 1374794, at *5 (finding
plaintiff's documentation did not reflect recognized national or international experts determine
qualifications for membership).
Accordingly, the Petitioner did not demonstrate the Beneficiary satisfies this criterion.

B. Judging
As indicated above, USCIS found the Petitioner established the Beneficiary's eligibility for this
criterion. Because the record does not support USCIS' favorable determination, we will withdraw that
decision.
The Petitioner provided letters from individuals who indicated they attended training courses in which
the Beneficiary served as an instructor. The letters claimed that the Beneficiary assessed their work.
For example, "[t]he training is intense, but the final evaluation is where [the Beneficiary] truly
exercises his authority" and "[the Beneficiary] individually assesses every applicant's work on critical
factors" (M-V-S), "[the Beneficiary] exercises complete discretion over who passes and who fails"
and "[h]]is decision is final and directly controls who is deemed qualified to work at the highest
professional level" (M-C-M-), and "[the Beneficiary] closely followed our work and personally
evaluated the repairs we performed" and "[h]]is judgment was based on his experience and on the
quality ofthe repair" (A-P-J-M-). In addition, the Petitioner submitted participation certificates signed
by the Beneficiary for various individuals who successfully completed the course, as well as a program
outline and brochure for the course.
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(4) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's participation on
a panel, or individually, as a judge of the work of others in the same or in an allied field of
specialization to that for which classification is sought." USCIS determines whether the person has
acted as the judge of the work of others in the same or an allied field of specialization. 5 Here, the
record reflects the Beneficiary's participation as an instructor for a course rather than as a judge. Cf.,
Oguntominiyi v. Garland, No. 4:24-CV-04252, 2026 WL 679247, at *5 (S.D. Tex. Mar. 4, 2026)
5 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
4
(rejecting the plaintiff's argument that assessing engineering projects clearly judges the work of
others); Onaghise v. Dep 't ofHomeland Sec., No. 3:20-CV-03033-X, 2022 WL 4073344, at *5 (N.D.
Tex. Sept. 2, 2022) (upholding letters indicating various responsibilities, including teaching, training,
and mentoring, did not constitute judging the work of others).
Similarly, the Petitioner presented a letter from S-Y-, owner of a dent repair company, thanking the
Beneficiary for training the staff "to significantly improve their skills, enhancing both the quality and
efficiency of the services provided by the company." However, the Petitioner did not demonstrate
how the letter shows the Beneficiary's participation as a judge of the work of others rather than as a
trainer.
For the reasons discussed above, the Petitioner did not establish the Beneficiary's participation as a
judge consistent with the plain language of this regulatory criterion. Because the Petitioner did not
show the Beneficiary's eligibility, we withdraw USCIS' favorable determination for this criterion.
